slides.title: Hashing
slides.raw:
Hashing
Message Digest 5 (MD5)
Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA)
Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC)
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: A one-way function that maps data to a fixed-size digest; commonly used for integrity verification and password storage.

course.learn: Hashing produces a fixed-size digest from input data using a one-way function. It is used to verify integrity and to store password verifiers when combined with appropriate password-hashing techniques.
course.why: If the input changes, the digest should change, allowing systems to detect tampering without needing the original content to be secret.
course.example: A downloaded ISO is hashed with SHA-256 and compared with the publisher's published digest.
course.exam: Hashing is not encryption: there is no decryption key. Hash comparison is an integrity clue.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: A salt is unique random data combined with a password before hashing. It ensures that two users with the same password do not end up with the same stored hash.
course.why: Salts make precomputed rainbow tables far less useful and force attackers to crack each password hash separately.
course.example: Two users both choose “Winter2026!”, but different salts produce different stored hashes.
course.exam: Salt does not need to be secret; uniqueness/randomness is the key property.
